MECI: Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction for Multimodal Entity Linking

Conference: Proceedings of the 49th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval; July 20–24, 2026; Melbourne, VIC, AustraliaProceedings of the 49th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR ’26), July 20–24, 2026, Melbourne, VIC, AustraliaDOI: 10.1145/3805712.3809583ISBN: 979-8-4007-2599-9/2026/07CCS: Information systems Specialized information retrievalCCS: Information systems Learning to rank
Jie Peng email: pengjie@nudt.edu.cn Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, Hunan, China , Yongxue Shan email: shanyongxue001@nudt.edu.cn Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, Hunan, China , Yongfu Zha email: zhayongfu@nudt.edu.cn Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, Hunan, China and Xiaodong Wang Note: Corresponding author. email: xdwang@nudt.edu.cn Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, Hunan, China

Abstract.

Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) aims to disambiguate mentions in multimodal contexts by grounding them to specific entities in a knowledge base. A pivotal challenge in MEL is capturing multi-level correspondences: the semantic consistency between mention-entity pairs and the complementary correlations across modalities. However, existing methods often suffer from element dominance due to their reliance on coupled interactions or coarse global aggregations. In response, we propose the Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction (MECI) framework. First, to capture multi-element mention-entity correspondences, we develop a Multi-view Experts Network that leverages a “divide-and-conquer” strategy for decoupled feature learning to mitigate element dominance, supported by a KL-guided routing mechanism that governs expert specialization and collaboration. Furthermore, to model cross-modal complementary correlations, we propose a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module, where a dynamic modality-aware weighting network refines interactions across hierarchical semantic levels, thereby integrating multi-granular evidence to counteract element dominance. Finally, we incorporate a generative semantic refinement stage that utilizes large language models for zero-shot re-ranking. Extensive experiments on WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL show that MECI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving Hits@1 by 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31%, respectively.

Keywords: 
Multimodal Entity Linking, Entity Linking, Multimodal Matching

1. Introduction

Entity Linking (EL) serves as a fundamental bridge connecting real-world information to knowledge bases. Over the past years, large efforts focused on text-based EL (Devlin et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020). However, images and text have become the most widely seen medium for publishing and understanding web information. Therefore, Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) (Hu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025) has emerged as a pivotal evolution, attracting attention from both academia and industry. By leveraging textual and visual cues, MEL plays a crucial role in knowledge-intensive applications such as semantic search (Liang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025), question answering (Marino et al., 2019; Xiong et al., 2019; Shah et al., 2019), and dialog systems (Ahmadvand et al., 2019; Liao et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025). As illustrated in Figure 1, given a multimodal mention, the MEL model aims to link it to the entity Canberra United in a multimodal knowledge base.

To effectively leverage multimodal information in MEL, a pivotal challenge is to identify and utilize the multi-element correspondences inherent in entity and mention contexts: 1) Multi-element correspondences between mentions and entities: Both the mention context and the entity representation often contain multiple consistent cues that facilitate semantic matching. As shown in Figure 1, the mention and the entity share textual elements such as Canberra, football, and University of Canberra. These correspondences highlight semantic similarities and provide explicit evidence for accurate entity linking, thereby reducing ambiguity and enhancing matching confidence. 2) Multi-element correspondences between modalities: The textual content and visual patches may exhibit correlative correspondences that are pivotal for comprehensive understanding. For instance, in Figure 1, the presence of a football in the image, combined with the textual context, helps definitively identify the entity as a football team—rather than a rugby or basketball team. Such cross-modal interactions allow textual and visual information to complement each other, enriching the model’s discriminative capacity for entity disambiguation.

To facilitate these multi-element correspondences, existing studies propose sophisticated correlative mechanisms, such as hierarchical gating mechanisms (Wang et al., 2022a; Sui et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2023), attention-based paradigms (Song et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024; Mi et al., 2025), graph-based aggregation schemes (Cao et al., 2018; Dongjie and Huang, 2022; Xing et al., 2023), and adaptive fusion strategies (Song et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2025b). Despite their progress, these methods face inherent challenges in handling the complexity of heterogeneous inputs. Specifically, hierarchical gating and attention-based approaches often employ coupled interaction designs across element levels (e.g., coupling coarse- and fine-grained semantics), which hinders adaptive adjustment to the characteristics of input semantics and readily leads to element dominance issues in the competition among heterogeneous features. Furthermore, graph-based and fusion approaches typically compress textual and visual features into a coarse global representation. This representation-level bottleneck makes it difficult to capture fine-grained, context-dependent associations, such as fine-grained visual correlations between entity and mention. In summary, existing designs tend to over-rely on prominent elements, leading to element dominance, where stronger modalities often overshadow weaker ones (modality dominance) or coarse global representations suppress fine-grained details (granularity bias). Such dependencies severely limit their capacity to model multi-element correspondences comprehensively, ultimately compromising entity linking accuracy in complex multimodal scenarios.

To mitigate these limitations and comprehensively capture multi-element correspondences, we propose the Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction (MECI) framework for multimodal entity linking. First, targeting the multi-element correspondences between mentions and entities, we introduce the Multi-view Experts Network (MVEN), which employs a “divide-and-conquer” strategy to capture both universal and view-specific characteristics. To regulate expert specialization and knowledge sharing, we propose a KL-guided routing mechanism that utilizes structural priors to adaptively coordinate information flow. Then, incorporating with a hierarchical matching strategy, MVEN provides specialized processing capacities for multi-element correlation analysis, effectively mitigating the element dominance problem. However, while MVEN effectively refines view-specific representations, these features remain relatively isolated. To bridge this gap and fully exploit the multi-element correspondences between modalities, we develop the Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module (HMIM). This module employs a dynamic cross-modal weighting network to refine interactions at distinct granularity levels—avoiding the granularity bias inherent in unified interaction paradigms—and utilizes a granularity-aware gating network to dynamically integrate multi-granular evidence for comprehensive cross-modal understanding. Finally, to further enhance linking precision, we introduce a finetuning-free generative semantic refinement stage, which reformulates candidate re-ranking as a zero-shot multiple-choice task to leverage the parametric knowledge of frozen Large Language Models (LLMs). In summary, our main contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose the Multi-view Experts Network for mention-entity correspondences. It employs a “divide-and-conquer” strategy with specialized routing and matching to decouple heterogeneous features, mitigating element dominance.

  • •

    We develop a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module for cross-modal correspondences. It employs dynamic weighting to avoid granularity bias and a gating network to incorporate multi-granular evidence.

  • •

    Experiments on WikiMEL, RichpediaMEL, and WikiDiverse demonstrate MECI’s superiority over state-of-the-art baselines, while ablation studies validate the efficacy of each proposed component.

2. Related Work

2.1. Text-based Entity Linking

Text-based Entity Linking (EL) aims to ground ambiguous textual mentions to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base. Generally, existing methodologies fall into two paradigms: local-level and global-level models. Local-level models (Wu et al., 2020; Devlin et al., 2019; Zhuang et al., 2021; Peters et al., 2019) focus on utilizing the immediate context, such as surrounding words or sentences, to aid disambiguation. In contrast, global-level models (Fang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019; Ran et al., 2018; Le and Titov, 2018) incorporate entity or topic coherence to ensure semantic consistency between mentions and entities. Nevertheless, these unimodal methods often struggle to effectively handle multimodal data that combines both textual and visual information.

2.2. Multimodal Entity Linking

Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) extends traditional entity linking by leveraging visual context for disambiguation. Its main goal is to map mentions in multimodal content to specific entities in a multimodal knowledge base. To address this, existing studies have proposed various sophisticated mechanisms, which can be broadly categorized into distinct paradigms. First, hierarchical gating mechanisms (Wang et al., 2022a; Sui et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2025b) and attention-based paradigms (Song et al., 2024; Mi et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025a) aim to refine feature matching through multi-level structures or cross-modal attention. However, these methods often employ coupled interaction designs, limiting their adaptability to varying input semantics and leading to element dominance. Meanwhile, graph-based aggregation schemes (Cao et al., 2018; Dongjie and Huang, 2022; Xing et al., 2023) explicitly model cross-modal relations as graphs, whereas adaptive fusion strategies (Yang et al., 2023; Song et al., 2025) aggregate features into unified representations. Despite their utility, these approaches tend to fuse information into global representations, making it difficult to capture fine-grained, context-dependent visual-textual associations. Recently, LLM-based methods (Shi et al., 2024; Long et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025) have achieved remarkable progress by leveraging the generative capabilities of large models, yet remain significantly constrained by excessive computational resource consumption. In summary, existing methods exhibit limitations in comprehensively modeling multi-element collaboration across modalities and granularities. Current designs tend to over-rely on prominent elements, causing modality dominance and granularity bias, which ultimately undermines linking performance in complex multimodal scenarios.

3. Methodology

3.1. Problem Formulation

MEL aims to resolve a mention mm to its target entity ee from a knowledge base ℰ\mathcal{E}. Formally, an entity is defined as a tuple e≜(et,ev)e\triangleq(e_{t},e_{v}), consisting of textual attributes ete_{t} and a visual representation eve_{v}. Similarly, a mention is modeled as m≜(mt,mv)m\triangleq(m_{t},m_{v}), containing the textual context mtm_{t} and an associated image mvm_{v}. To align mentions with entities, the model parameters θ\theta are optimized to maximize the likelihood of the ground-truth on the training set 𝒟\mathcal{D}:

(1) θ∗=arg⁡max⁡∑(m,e)∈𝒟θ⁡log⁡pθ​(e|m,ℰ)\theta^{*}=\arg\max_{\theta}\sum_{(m,e)\in\mathcal{D}}\log p_{\theta}(e|m,\mathcal{E})

Here, pθ​(e|m,ℰ)p_{\theta}(e|m,\mathcal{E}) serves as a similarity metric to evaluate the relevance of a candidate entity ee to the query mention mm.

3.2. Feature Encoding

To initialize the representations for the entity ee and mention mm, the model encodes their associated textual and visual information, as illustrated in Figure 2 (step 1). Specifically, the framework leverages the pre-trained CLIP model (specifically CLIP-ViT-Base-Patch32). We utilize its text encoder (EncT\text{Enc}^{T}) for textual feature extraction and its image encoder (EncV\text{Enc}^{V}) for visual feature encoding:

(2) 𝑯mT,𝑯mV\displaystyle\boldsymbol{H}_{m}^{T},\boldsymbol{H}_{m}^{V} =EncT​(mt),EncV​(mv)\displaystyle=\text{Enc}^{T}(m_{t}),\text{Enc}^{V}(m_{v})
𝑯eT,𝑯eV\displaystyle\boldsymbol{H}_{e}^{T},\boldsymbol{H}_{e}^{V} =EncT​(et),EncV​(ev)\displaystyle=\text{Enc}^{T}(e_{t}),\text{Enc}^{V}(e_{v})

where 𝑯mT∈ℝL1×d\boldsymbol{H}_{m}^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{1}\times d} and 𝑯eT∈ℝL2×d\boldsymbol{H}_{e}^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{2}\times d} represent the token-level textual sequences (lengths L1,L2L_{1},L_{2}), while 𝑯mV∈ℝP1×d\boldsymbol{H}_{m}^{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{P_{1}\times d} and 𝑯eV∈ℝP2×d\boldsymbol{H}_{e}^{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{P_{2}\times d} denote the patch-level visual sequences (patch counts P1,P2P_{1},P_{2}). Beyond these fine-grained representations, we extract coarse-grained global vectors 𝒉mT,𝒉eT,𝒉mV,𝒉eV\boldsymbol{h}_{m}^{T},\boldsymbol{h}_{e}^{T},\boldsymbol{h}_{m}^{V},\boldsymbol{h}_{e}^{V} to capture comprehensive semantic context. These are obtained via the output of the special [EOS] token from EncT\text{Enc}^{T} and the [CLS] token from EncV\text{Enc}^{V}, respectively.

3.3. Multi-view Experts Network

To effectively model multi-element correspondences between mentions and entities, we recognize that inputs of varying modalities and granularities offer diverse and complementary evidence from distinct perspectives. However, existing strategies, such as feature-coupled interactions (Mi et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025b) or global alignment (Yang et al., 2023; Song et al., 2025), often suffer from element dominance, thereby struggling to comprehensively capture these dependencies.

To address these challenges, we propose the Multi-view Experts Network (MVEN). By adopting a decoupled representation learning paradigm, MVEN ensures specialized processing capabilities for heterogeneous features, thereby effectively mitigating element dominance. Specifically, MVEN comprises three key components: (1) a View-Specific Experts Module employing a “Divide-and-Conquer” strategy to capture universal patterns and view-specific characteristics; (2) a KL-Guided Routing Mechanism introducing structural priors to balance expert specialization and knowledge sharing; and (3) a Gated Aggregation and Matching Layer that dynamically fuses expert signals and performs specialized correlations computation across diverse perspectives.

3.3.1. View-Specific Experts Module

To capture semantic information, we adopt a “Divide-and-Conquer” strategy to model both common patterns and view-specific characteristics.

Universal Semantic Projection. Formally, we formulate each expert unit E⁡(⋅)E(\cdot) as a learnable transformation comprising a linear projection, normalization, and activation. Let 𝑯=[𝒉T;𝑯T;𝒉V;𝑯V]∈ℝN×d\boldsymbol{H}=[\boldsymbol{h}^{T};\boldsymbol{H}^{T};\boldsymbol{h}^{V};\boldsymbol{H}^{V}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} denote the multimodal input features for either a mention or an entity. Based on this, we employ a shared expert mechanism to extract view-agnostic semantic structures. Accordingly, for any arbitrary input token 𝒉i∈ℝd\boldsymbol{h}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the universal expert Eu​(⋅)E_{u}(\cdot) projects it into a unified semantic space:

(3) 𝒛𝒮​(𝒉i)=Eu​(𝒉i)=g⁡(LayerNorm​(𝒉i​𝑾u+𝒃u))\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathcal{S}}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i})=E_{u}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i})=g\left(\text{LayerNorm}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i}\boldsymbol{W}_{u}+\boldsymbol{b}_{u})\right)

where 𝑾u\boldsymbol{W}_{u} and 𝒃u\boldsymbol{b}_{u} denote the learnable parameters, and g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) represents a non-linear activation function (such as ReLU).

Collaborative Intra-Expert Fusion. To capture the inherent characteristics unique to each perspective, we establish two distinct expert pools: a modality expert set Φℳ={Emℳ}m=1Km\Phi^{\mathcal{M}}=\{E^{\mathcal{M}}_{m}\}_{m=1}^{K_{m}} and a granularity expert set Φ𝒢={Eg𝒢}g=1Kg\Phi^{\mathcal{G}}=\{E^{\mathcal{G}}_{g}\}_{g=1}^{K_{g}}. Despite the greater number of fine-grained tokens, we maintain an equal number of experts for both granularities. This symmetric design ensures balanced interaction and prevents potential fusion bias from imbalanced expert scales. To enrich the representation of a specific view without compromising its distinctiveness, we propose a Collaborative Intra-Expert Fusion mechanism. For a given sample 𝒉i\boldsymbol{h}_{i} belonging to category 𝒱∈{ℳ,𝒢}\mathcal{V}\in\{\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G}\}, let vv denote its ground-truth view index (e.g., a specific modality ID). The fused representation 𝒛𝒱​(𝒉i)\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathcal{V}}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i}) is computed as a dynamic weighted aggregation:

(4) 𝒛𝒱​(𝒉i)=β𝒱(i)​Ev𝒱​(𝒉i)+1−β𝒱(i)|Φ𝒱|−1​∑Ek𝒱∈Φ𝒱,k≠vEk𝒱​(𝒉i)\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathcal{V}}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i})=\beta_{\mathcal{V}}^{(i)}E^{\mathcal{V}}_{v}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i})+\frac{1-\beta_{\mathcal{V}}^{(i)}}{|\Phi^{\mathcal{V}}|-1}\sum_{E^{\mathcal{V}}_{k}\in\Phi^{\mathcal{V}},k\neq v}E^{\mathcal{V}}_{k}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i})

where Ev𝒱E^{\mathcal{V}}_{v} represents the native expert corresponding to the sample’s identity, and the summation term incorporates complementary knowledge from peer experts within the same pool. The coefficient β𝒱(i)∈(0,1)\beta_{\mathcal{V}}^{(i)}\in(0,1) acts as a dynamic trade-off parameter, governing the balance between preserving native specificity and incorporating external knowledge.

3.3.2. KL-Guided Routing Mechanism

The efficacy of the above collaborative fusion depends significantly on the routing mechanism that determines the trade-off coefficient β𝒱(i)\beta_{\mathcal{V}}^{(i)}. Thus, we introduce a KL-Guided Routing Mechanism, a novel approach that leverages structural priors to regularize the routing distribution. Specifically, for each input token 𝒉i\boldsymbol{h}_{i}, we first identify its categorical identity: let yℳ(i)y_{\mathcal{M}}^{(i)} and y𝒢(i)y_{\mathcal{G}}^{(i)} denote its ground-truth modality and granularity indices, respectively. Instead of employing these as rigid one-hot targets, we construct “Soft Target” distributions 𝒯\mathcal{T} to serve as regularizers. This is achieved by applying temperature scaling τ\tau to the one-hot vectors 𝐞y\mathbf{e}_{y}:

(5) 𝒯ℳ(i)=Softmax​(𝐞yℳ(i)τℳ),𝒯𝒢(i)=Softmax​(𝐞y𝒢(i)τ𝒢)\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{(i)}=\text{Softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{e}_{y_{\mathcal{M}}^{(i)}}}{\tau_{\mathcal{M}}}\right),\quad\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{G}}^{(i)}=\text{Softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{e}_{y_{\mathcal{G}}^{(i)}}}{\tau_{\mathcal{G}}}\right)

where 𝐞y\mathbf{e}_{y} denotes the one-hot vector for index yy. The temperature τ\tau modulates the prior’s focus: a lower τ\tau sharpens the distribution to enforce expert specialization, while a higher τ\tau flattens it to encourage inter-expert collaboration and knowledge sharing.

Simultaneously, for each input 𝒉i\boldsymbol{h}_{i}, the router predicts the routing distributions 𝒫𝒱\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{V}} via learnable projections:

(6) 𝒫𝒱(i)=Softmax​(𝒉i​𝑾𝒱+𝒃𝒱),𝒱∈{ℳ,𝒢}\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{V}}^{(i)}=\text{Softmax}\left(\boldsymbol{h}_{i}\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathcal{V}}+\boldsymbol{b}_{\mathcal{V}}\right),\quad\mathcal{V}\in\{\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G}\}

where 𝑾𝒱\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathcal{V}} and 𝒃𝒱\boldsymbol{b}_{\mathcal{V}} are learnable parameters of the routing network.

To align the learned policy with our structural priors while permitting data-driven adaptation, we minimize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the predicted distribution 𝒫\mathcal{P} and the soft target 𝒯\mathcal{T}:

(7) ℒroute\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{route}} =12​N​∑i=1N[DKL​(𝒯ℳ(i)∥𝒫ℳ(i))+DKL​(𝒯𝒢(i)∥𝒫𝒢(i))]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[D_{\text{KL}}\left(\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{(i)}\middle\|\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}^{(i)}\right)+D_{\text{KL}}\left(\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{G}}^{(i)}\middle\|\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{G}}^{(i)}\right)\right]
=12​N​∑i=1N∑𝒱∈{ℳ,𝒢}∑k=1K𝒱𝒯𝒱,k(i)​log⁡𝒯𝒱,k(i)𝒫𝒱,k(i)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\mathcal{V}\in\{\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G}\}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{\mathcal{V}}}\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V},k}^{(i)}\log\frac{\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V},k}^{(i)}}{\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{V},k}^{(i)}}

where K𝒱K_{\mathcal{V}} denotes the number of experts in category 𝒱\mathcal{V} (i.e., KℳK_{\mathcal{M}} and K𝒢K_{\mathcal{G}}).

This formulation aligns the router with semantic priors while preserving input context-driven flexibility. By softening 𝒯\mathcal{T} via the temperature mechanism, the model assigns non-zero probabilities to peer experts, thus avoiding the knowledge isolation typical of hard routing. Finally, the dynamic trade-off coefficient is instantiated as the predicted probability of the native expert: β𝒱(i)=𝒫𝒱,v(i)\beta_{\mathcal{V}}^{(i)}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{V},v}^{(i)}, where v=y𝒱(i)v=y_{\mathcal{V}}^{(i)}.

3.3.3. Gated Inter-Expert Aggregation

Building upon the universal (𝒛𝒮\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathcal{S}}), modality-specific (𝒛ℳ\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathcal{M}}), and granularity-specific (𝒛𝒢\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathcal{G}}) representations, we introduce a Gated Inter-Expert Aggregation strategy to integrate these heterogeneous signals. Specifically, for an input token 𝒉i\boldsymbol{h}_{i}, we determine the salience of each expert category 𝒱∈{ℳ,𝒢}\mathcal{V}\in\{\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G}\} by computing gating coefficients:

(8) λ𝒱(i)=σ⁡((𝒘𝒱g)⊤​𝒛𝒱​(𝒉i)+b𝒱g)\lambda_{\mathcal{V}}^{(i)}=\sigma\left((\boldsymbol{w}_{\mathcal{V}}^{g})^{\top}\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathcal{V}}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i})+b_{\mathcal{V}}^{g}\right)

These coefficients adaptively modulate expert contributions to produce the fused representation:

(9) 𝒛ℱ​(𝒉i)=𝒛𝒮​(𝒉i)+λℳ(i)​𝒛ℳ​(𝒉i)+λ𝒢(i)​𝒛𝒢​(𝒉i)\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathcal{F}}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i})=\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathcal{S}}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i})+\lambda_{\mathcal{M}}^{(i)}\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathcal{M}}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i})+\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}^{(i)}\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{h}_{i})

This residual-like formulation maintains a stable universal foundation while flexibly incorporating evidence tailored to the specific context. Consequently, the final representations for a mention mm and a candidate entity ee are constructed as the concatenation of all view-specific features: 𝒁m/e=[𝒛T;𝒁T;𝒛V;𝒁V]m/e\boldsymbol{Z}_{m/e}=[\boldsymbol{z}^{T};\boldsymbol{Z}^{T};\boldsymbol{z}^{V};\boldsymbol{Z}^{V}]_{m/e}.

3.3.4. Hierarchical Matching Strategy

To accommodate the distinct matching requirements of heterogeneous perspectives, we categorize the full view set into global views Ωg={Tg,Vg}\Omega_{g}=\{T_{g},V_{g}\} and local views Ωl={Tl,Vl}\Omega_{l}=\{T_{l},V_{l}\}, where TT and VV denote textual and visual modalities, and subscripts gg and ll represent global and local granularities, respectively. For global views v∈Ωgv\in\Omega_{g}, we prioritize Global Semantic Coherence. Given the global feature vectors 𝒛mv\boldsymbol{z}_{m}^{v} and 𝒛ev\boldsymbol{z}_{e}^{v}, we compute their correlation via cosine similarity:

(10) sglobalv=cos⁡(𝒛mv,𝒛ev)=(𝒛mv)⊤​𝒛ev‖𝒛mv‖2​‖𝒛ev‖2s_{\mathrm{global}}^{v}=\cos(\boldsymbol{z}_{m}^{v},\boldsymbol{z}_{e}^{v})=\frac{(\boldsymbol{z}_{m}^{v})^{\top}\boldsymbol{z}_{e}^{v}}{\|\boldsymbol{z}_{m}^{v}\|_{2}\,\|\boldsymbol{z}_{e}^{v}\|_{2}}

Conversely, for fine-grained views v∈Ωlv\in\Omega_{l}, we employ a Local Evidence Accumulation layer. Given local feature sequences 𝒁mv\boldsymbol{Z}_{m}^{v} and 𝒁ev\boldsymbol{Z}_{e}^{v}, we first construct context-aware entity prototypes 𝒁~ev\tilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}_{e}^{v} via attention-based aggregation: 𝒁~ev=Softmax​(𝒁mv​(𝒁ev)⊤/d)​𝒁ev\tilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}_{e}^{v}=\text{Softmax}(\boldsymbol{Z}_{m}^{v}(\boldsymbol{Z}_{e}^{v})^{\top}/\sqrt{d})\boldsymbol{Z}_{e}^{v}. This mechanism dynamically aligns entity features with the mention context, effectively highlighting relevant evidence segments while suppressing noise. The local score is then obtained by averaging the cosine similarity at each local position:

(11) slocalv=1Lv​∑i=1Lv(𝒛m,iv)⊤​𝒛~e,iv‖𝒛m,iv‖2​‖𝒛~e,iv‖2s_{\mathrm{local}}^{v}=\frac{1}{L_{v}}\sum_{i=1}^{L_{v}}\frac{(\boldsymbol{z}_{m,i}^{v})^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{z}}_{e,i}^{v}}{\|\boldsymbol{z}_{m,i}^{v}\|_{2}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{z}}_{e,i}^{v}\|_{2}}

Finally, the comprehensive similarity ses_{e} is derived by averaging the matching scores across all global and local views:

(12) se=∑v∈Ωgsglobalv+∑v∈Ωlslocalv|Ωg|+|Ωl|s_{e}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{v\in\Omega_{g}}s_{\mathrm{global}}^{v}+\displaystyle\sum_{v\in\Omega_{l}}s_{\mathrm{local}}^{v}}{|\Omega_{g}|+|\Omega_{l}|}

3.4. Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction

While the Multi-view Experts Network effectively models mention-entity correlations through decoupled representations, these view-specific features remain relatively isolated, limiting the model’s ability to capture multi-element correspondences between modalities. To bridge this gap, we develop the Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module (HMIM). HMIM first employs a Dynamic Cross-modal Weighting Network (DCWN) to refine interactions at distinct granularities. Subsequently, a Granularity-aware Gating Network dynamically fuses the multi-granular evidence into a robust joint representation for precise matching.

3.4.1. Dynamic Cross-modal Weighting Network

The DCWN processes fine-grained and coarse-grained streams in parallel to model intricate cross-modal dependencies. This hierarchical strategy effectively avoids the granularity bias inherent in unified interaction paradigms, where multi-level features are concatenated without structural distinction. We describe the operation using the fine-grained token stream as an illustrative example. Let 𝑯=[𝒁T;𝒁V]∈ℝL×d\boldsymbol{H}=[\boldsymbol{Z}^{T};\boldsymbol{Z}^{V}]\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} denote the input sequence combining textual and visual local tokens derived from the previous module. We employ a multi-head cross-modal attention mechanism with NhN_{h} heads to model pairwise correspondences. For the ii-th head (i=1,…,Nhi=1,\dots,N_{h}), the input is projected into query, key, and value subspaces via learnable matrices: 𝑸(i)=𝑯​𝑾Q(i)\boldsymbol{Q}^{(i)}=\boldsymbol{H}\boldsymbol{W}_{Q}^{(i)}, 𝑲(i)=𝑯​𝑾K(i)\boldsymbol{K}^{(i)}=\boldsymbol{H}\boldsymbol{W}_{K}^{(i)}, and 𝑽(i)=𝑯​𝑾V(i)\boldsymbol{V}^{(i)}=\boldsymbol{H}\boldsymbol{W}_{V}^{(i)}, where 𝑾Q(i),𝑾K(i),𝑾V(i)∈ℝd×dh\boldsymbol{W}_{Q}^{(i)},\boldsymbol{W}_{K}^{(i)},\boldsymbol{W}_{V}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{h}}.

The attention matrix 𝑨(i)∈ℝL×L\boldsymbol{A}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L} captures the pairwise correspondences between tokens and is computed as:

(13) 𝑨n,j(i)=exp⁡((𝑸n(i))⊤​𝑲j(i)/dh)∑k=1Lexp⁡((𝑸n(i))⊤​𝑲k(i)/dh)\boldsymbol{A}_{n,j}^{(i)}=\frac{\exp\left((\boldsymbol{Q}_{n}^{(i)})^{\top}\boldsymbol{K}_{j}^{(i)}/\sqrt{d_{h}}\right)}{\sum_{k=1}^{L}\exp\left((\boldsymbol{Q}_{n}^{(i)})^{\top}\boldsymbol{K}_{k}^{(i)}/\sqrt{d_{h}}\right)}

The context-enriched output is derived by aggregating the values weighted by 𝑨(i)\boldsymbol{A}^{(i)}, followed by concatenation and a linear projection 𝑾O\boldsymbol{W}_{O}:

(14) 𝑯~=LayerNorm​((⨁i=1Nh𝑨(i)​𝑽(i))​𝑾O+𝑯)\tilde{\boldsymbol{H}}=\text{LayerNorm}\left(\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^{N_{h}}\boldsymbol{A}^{(i)}\boldsymbol{V}^{(i)}\right)\boldsymbol{W}_{O}+\boldsymbol{H}\right)

Crucially, to explicitly quantify the reliability of cross-modal correspondences and refine the features, we introduce a Token Confidence Estimation (TCE) mechanism. Rather than treating all tokens equally, TCE computes a scalar confidence score wnw_{n} for each token nn, reflecting its saliency within the multimodal context. This is formulated by aggregating the attention scores across all heads and tokens:

(15) wn=exp⁡(1L⋅Nh​∑j=1L∑i=1Nh𝑨j,n(i))∑k=1Lexp⁡(1L⋅Nh​∑j=1L∑i=1Nh𝑨j,k(i))w_{n}=\frac{\exp\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{L\cdot N_{h}}}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{h}}\boldsymbol{A}_{j,n}^{(i)}\right)}{\sum_{k=1}^{L}\exp\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{L\cdot N_{h}}}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{h}}\boldsymbol{A}_{j,k}^{(i)}\right)}

This mechanism acts as a soft attention filter, adaptively emphasizing tokens that exhibit strong semantic consistency. The final granularity-specific representation is obtained by re-weighting the enhanced features:

(16) 𝒛l=∑n=1Lwnl​𝒉~nl,𝒛g=∑n=1L′wng​𝒉~ng\boldsymbol{z}_{l}=\sum_{n=1}^{L}w_{n}^{l}\tilde{\boldsymbol{h}}_{n}^{l},\quad\boldsymbol{z}_{g}=\sum_{n=1}^{L^{\prime}}w_{n}^{g}\tilde{\boldsymbol{h}}_{n}^{g}

where 𝒛l\boldsymbol{z}_{l} and 𝒛g\boldsymbol{z}_{g} denote the aggregated fine-grained (local) and coarse-grained (global) representations, respectively (with L′L^{\prime} denoting the length of the global stream).

3.4.2. Granularity-aware Gating Network

To effectively integrate the refined multi-granular evidence from 𝒛g\boldsymbol{z}_{g} and 𝒛l\boldsymbol{z}_{l}, the Granularity-aware Gating Network dynamically fuses them into a robust joint representation. We compute granularity-aware gating scores αk\alpha_{k} for k∈{g,l}k\in\{g,l\} via:

(17) αk=exp⁡(𝒘g⊤​tanh⁡(𝑾k​𝒛k))∑j∈{g,l}exp⁡(𝒘g⊤​tanh⁡(𝑾j​𝒛j))\alpha_{k}=\frac{\exp\left(\boldsymbol{w}_{g}^{\top}\tanh(\boldsymbol{W}_{k}\boldsymbol{z}_{k})\right)}{\sum_{j\in\{g,l\}}\exp\left(\boldsymbol{w}_{g}^{\top}\tanh(\boldsymbol{W}_{j}\boldsymbol{z}_{j})\right)}

where 𝑾k\boldsymbol{W}_{k} and 𝒘g\boldsymbol{w}_{g} are learnable parameters. The unified representation 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} is then derived through a weighted aggregation:

(18) 𝒖=αg​𝒛g+αl​𝒛l\boldsymbol{u}=\alpha_{g}\boldsymbol{z}_{g}+\alpha_{l}\boldsymbol{z}_{l}

This mechanism enables the model to selectively emphasize the granularity that is most informative for the current context. Finally, the matching score is computed as the cosine similarity between the unified mention and entity representations:

(19) sc=cos⁡(𝒖m,𝒖e)=𝒖m⊤​𝒖e‖𝒖m‖​‖𝒖e‖s_{c}=\cos(\boldsymbol{u}_{m},\boldsymbol{u}_{e})=\frac{\boldsymbol{u}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{u}_{e}}{\|\boldsymbol{u}_{m}\|\|\boldsymbol{u}_{e}\|}

3.5. Optimization and Generative Refinement

3.5.1. Holistic Training Objectives

We employ a multi-perspective contrastive learning paradigm (Luo et al., 2023) to enforce discriminative alignment across both individual and fused perspectives. Specifically, we apply contrastive constraints to three distinct scoring components: the expert-based score ses_{e}, the interaction-based score scs_{c}, and the overall consensus score so=se+scs_{o}=s_{e}+s_{c}. The InfoNCE loss ℒϕ\mathcal{L}_{\phi} for a given scoring function sϕs_{\phi} (where ϕ∈{e,c,o}\phi\in\{e,c,o\}) is defined as:

(20) ℒϕ=−𝔼⁡[log⁡exp⁡(sϕ​(m,e))exp⁡(sϕ​(m,e))+∑e′∈𝒩mexp⁡(sϕ​(m,e′))]\mathcal{L}_{\phi}=-\mathbb{E}\left[\log\frac{\exp(s_{\phi}(m,e))}{\exp(s_{\phi}(m,e))+\sum_{e^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}_{m}}\exp(s_{\phi}(m,e^{\prime}))}\right]

where 𝒩m\mathcal{N}_{m} denotes the set of negative samples corresponding to the anchor mm. The total objective aggregates these matching losses with the routing regularization term:

(21) ℒtotal=∑ϕ∈{e,c,o}ℒϕ+λ​ℒroute\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\sum_{\phi\in\{e,c,o\}}\mathcal{L}_{\phi}+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{route}}

where λ\lambda governs the weight of the KL-divergence constraint. This formulation ensures that the model learns robust representations while strictly adhering to the semantic structural priors imposed on the router.

3.5.2. LLM-based Generative Reasoning

Inspired by (Liu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024), we incorporate a Generative Semantic Refinement stage to further enhance entity linking precision. Initially, a candidate set 𝒞m\mathcal{C}_{m} is retrieved based on the top-KK scores sos_{o}:

(22) 𝒞m=arg​topKe∈ℰ⁡(so​(m,e))\mathcal{C}_{m}=\operatorname*{arg\,topK}_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\big(s_{o}(m,e)\big)

Subsequently, the refinement stage is reformulated as a multiple-choice problem. By constructing a prompt ℐ⁡(m,𝒞m)\mathcal{I}(m,\mathcal{C}_{m}) that integrates the mention context tmt_{m} and candidate descriptions {te}\{t_{e}\}—as illustrated in the prompt design in Figure 2 (step 4)—the optimal entity e∗e^{*} is determined by maximizing the LLM’s generation probability:

(23) e∗=argmaxe∈𝒞mℙLLM​(e∣ℐ⁡(m,𝒞m);Θ)e^{*}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{e\in\mathcal{C}_{m}}\,\mathbb{P}_{\text{LLM}}\Big(e\mid\mathcal{I}(m,\mathcal{C}_{m});\Theta\Big)

where Θ\Theta denotes frozen LLM parameters. This way effectively leverages parametric knowledge to pinpoint the ground-truth entity.

4. Evaluation

In this section, we evaluate our proposed MECI through comprehensive experiments on three public MEL datasets, accompanied by extensive analyses to provide deeper insights into our framework.

4.1. Experimental Setup

4.1.1. Datasets

To evaluate our approach, we utilize three established datasets: WikiDiverse (Wang et al., 2022b), WikiMEL (Wang et al., 2022a), and RichpediaMEL (Wang et al., 2022a). Derived from Wikipedia entity pages, WikiMEL targets Wikidata as its knowledge base and consists of over 22,000 multimodal sentences, focusing predominantly on Person entities. In contrast, WikiDiverse is sourced from Wikinews and maps to Wikipedia; it spans seven distinct entity categories, including Person, Organization, Location, Country, Event, Works, and Misc. RichpediaMEL integrates Wikidata attributes for entities found in Richpedia (Wang et al., 2019) with multimodal content from Wikipedia. Regarding data partitioning, we adopt the standard split configurations: an 8:1:1 ratio for WikiDiverse, and a 7:1:2 ratio for both WikiMEL and RichMEL. The statistics of these datasets are shown in Table 1.

4.1.2. Baselines and Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate our method against three groups of representative baselines: (1) Text-based EL methods, such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), and BLINK (Wu et al., 2020); (2) Discriminative MEL methods, covering CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), ViLT (Kim et al., 2021), ALBEF (Li et al., 2021), METER (Dou et al., 2022), GHMFC (Wang et al., 2022a), MIMIC (Luo et al., 2023), OT-MEL (Zhang et al., 2024), MELOV (Sui et al., 2024), M3EL (Hu et al., 2025a), and MMOE (Hu et al., 2025b); and (3) LLM-based methods, including GEMEL (Shi et al., 2024), UniMEL (Liu et al., 2024), IIER (Mi et al., 2025), and I2CR (Liu et al., 2025). To assess model performance, we utilize two standard metrics: Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and Hits@NN. MRR calculates the average of the reciprocal ranks of the first correct answer. Hits@NN reports the percentage of test cases where the correct entity appears within the top NN predictions, where N∈{1,3,5}N\in\{1,3,5\}.

4.1.3. Implementations

We conducted the experiments on a workstation equipped with an Intel Core i9-12900K CPU (64GB RAM) and two NVIDIA A100 GPUs (2x40GB). we employ the pre-trained CLIP-Vit-Base-Patch32 (Radford et al., 2021) model as the initialization of the textual and visual encoder. For input preprocessing, visual inputs were resized to a resolution of 224×224224\times 224. Subsequently, the maximum sequence length was set to 50 tokens for both visual and textual inputs. A unified training configuration was maintained across all datasets. The models were optimized using AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with a batch size of 64 for 20 epochs. The learning rate was initialized at 5×10−65\times 10^{-6} for WikiMEL and 1×10−51\times 10^{-5} for both the WikiDiverse and RichpediaMEL datasets. In the re-ranking phase, we utilized DeepSeek-v3 to re-rank the retrieved candidates, setting the candidate pool size to K=16K=16. Our code is available at MEL-MECI-main.

4.2. Main Results

The comparative results on three MEL datasets are summarized in Table 2. Overall, our proposed MECI framework demonstrates superior performance across all benchmarks. Specifically, our MECI consistently outperforms previous strong discriminative models, while our zero-shot generative refinement model MECI+ achieves new state-of-the-art results. The detailed analysis is as follows:

⊳\triangleright Comparison with Text-based Methods. Text-based EL consistently underperforms multimodal approaches. The best text-only model achieves only 74.82% Hits@1 on WikiMEL compared to over 90% for our method. This suggests these text-based EL baselines struggle to capture deep semantics. Our approach addresses this by learning richer representations from both textual context and auxiliary visual signals.

⊳\triangleright Comparison with Discriminative MEL Methods. Compared to state-of-the-art discriminative baselines like MMOE and M3EL, our MECI achieves consistent superiority, surpassing the strongest baseline MMOE by 5.34%, 1.27%, and 1.31% in Hits@1 on WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL, respectively. This comes from our collaborative design: MVEN employs a “divide-and-conquer” strategy to decouple subspaces and mitigate element dominance, while HMIM utilizes a granularity-dependent cross-modal weighting network to capture intricate cross-modal dependencies. In contrast to baselines limited by coupled interactions or coarse global fusion, MECI effectively alleviates element dominance, capturing comprehensive multi-element correspondences.

⊳\triangleright Comparison with Generative Methods. Finally, we benchmark MECI+ (MECI augmented with a zero-shot generative refinement stage) against LLM-based paradigms. While I2CR exhibits competitive performance, our zero-shot MECI+ surpasses the strongest baseline by large margins of 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31% in Hits@1 across the three datasets, respectively. Crucially, our model realizes these gains without the need for resource-intensive fine-tuning. By leveraging a frozen DeepSeek V3 to re-rank candidates via a multiple-choice prompting strategy, we demonstrate that a robust retrieval foundation is sufficient to effectively elicit the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

⊳\triangleright Low Resource Setting. We further examine model performance under data-constrained settings (10% and 20% training data) to address the challenge of costly data annotation. As shown in Figure 3, our method consistently surpasses baselines M3EL and MMOE. Note that the MMOE baseline was reproduced by omitting the DME mention text augmentation to ensure comparable input configurations. Even in the challenging 10% setting, our framework maintains high performance: it achieves 74.1% accuracy on WikiDiverse (vs. 69.7% for MMOE) and 81.5% Hits@1 on RichpediaMEL (vs. 80.1% for MMOE and 69.5% for M3EL). These significant margins attest to the data efficiency of our approach, highlighting its potential for applications where labeled data is scarce.

4.3. Ablation Study

We examine the contribution of specific components through ablation studies on all datasets (Table 3), covering three main aspects:

⊳\triangleright Impact of Multi-view Experts Network. As shown in Table 3, removing the MVEN module leads to the most significant performance degradation, with a sharp drop of 7.46% in Hits@1 on the WikiDiverse dataset. This empirical evidence strongly supports our “Divide-and-Conquer” strategy, indicating that aggregating diverse views is critical for capturing comprehensive evidence. Specifically, ablating the grain expert, which is designed to capture distinctive granularity-specific semantics, causes a Hits@1 decline of 3.32%. Similarly, the modal expert, responsible for extracting distinctive modality-specific semantics, contributes a notable gain of 2.69%. Even the shared expert, aimed at modeling common underlying patterns across views to bridge semantic gaps, brings a consistent improvement of 1.16%. These results confirm that each expert plays an indispensable and complementary role in robust entity linking.

⊳\triangleright Effectiveness of Hierarchical Interaction. Removing the HMIM module (w/o hierarchical multimodal interaction) results in an observable performance drop, e.g., decreasing Hits@1 by 1.86% on WikiMEL. This indicates that the HMIM module is essential for modeling deep cross-modal dependencies. Crucially, replacing our hierarchical design with a flat interaction mechanism (repl. granularity unified interaction)—where fine-grained and coarse-grained features are concatenated for unified DCWN attention processing—yields suboptimal results with a 2.15% deficit on WikiMEL. This validates the effectiveness of our granularity-specific interaction module, avoiding the granularity bias caused by unified processing.

⊳\triangleright Analysis of Optimization and Visual Modality. Regarding optimization, for instance, the sharp 10.47% Hits@1 drop on RichpediaMEL without ℒe\mathcal{L}_{e} (w/o expert-based matching) emphasizes the need for direct supervision on expert-based matching, while declines without ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} and ℒo\mathcal{L}_{o} validate our interaction-based matching and overall consensus matching objective. Notably, removing ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} and removing the HMIM module correspond to the same ablation setting. Crucially, omitting ℒroute\mathcal{L}_{\text{route}} (w/o router loss) confirms that KL-guided priors are essential for regularization. These priors enforce a critical balance between specialization and collaboration that unconstrained adaptation lacks. Furthermore, the performance drop with a hard router (repl. hard router) validates our approach: its discrete nature hinders effective expert combination, whereas our differentiable gating smoothly synthesizes diverse capabilities. Finally, the consistent performance drop without visual features (w/o visual modality)—exemplified by a 5.27% decrease on WikiMEL—highlights the necessity of complementary visual evidence.

4.4. Parameter Sensitivity Analysis

⊳\triangleright Effect of Loss Weight λ\lambda. Figure 4 presents the impact of the routing loss weight λ\lambda on model performance. We observe that the performance improves as λ\lambda increases from small values, confirming the effectiveness of our KL-guided routing mechanism in regulating expert behaviors. The model achieves optimal results at λ=0.01\lambda=0.01 for WikiDiverse and λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 for RichpediaEML. However, further increasing λ\lambda leads to performance degradation. This is likely because an excessive weight on ℒroute\mathcal{L}_{\text{route}} over-constrains the routing network, hindering the model’s ability to learn flexible representations for entity matching.

⊳\triangleright Effect of Temperature τℳ\tau_{\mathcal{M}} and τ𝒢\tau_{\mathcal{G}}. We further investigate the joint impact of temperature hyperparameters τℳ\tau_{\mathcal{M}} and τ𝒢\tau_{\mathcal{G}} on model performance across the WikiDiverse and WikiMEL datasets, as illustrated in Figure 5. From the figure, the overall trend indicates that the model achieves optimal or near-optimal performance when both temperatures are set to moderate values (e.g., 1.01.0, 0.50.5). This pattern is particularly pronounced in the WikiDiverse dataset. Deviating from this range results in performance degradation, which corroborates our design rationale. Specifically, extremely low temperatures (e.g., 0.050.05) induce rigid, deterministic routing that hinders necessary cross-expert knowledge sharing. Conversely, excessively high temperatures (e.g., 5.05.0) lead to an overly uniform distribution—similar to a standard soft router—which weakens expert specialization and dilutes domain-specific information. based on these empirical findings, we observe a peak Hit@1 of 79.93% on WikiDiverse when both temperatures are set to 1.01.0, and 90.38% on WikiMEL with τℳ=0.5\tau_{\mathcal{M}}=0.5 and τ𝒢=0.1\tau_{\mathcal{G}}=0.1.

4.5. Further Discussion

⊳\triangleright Analysis of Generative Semantic Refinement. To assess the efficacy and universality of the generative semantic refinement stage, we conducted evaluations using three distinct LLMs: DeepSeek v3 (text-only LLM), GPT-4o (multimodal LLM), and the locally deployable Qwen3-8B. As illustrated in Figure 6, integrating this refinement strategy yields consistent performance improvements on all baselines, and our proposed framework robustly outperforms two baseline methods (M3EL and MMOE) across all LLM backbones. Among the tested models, DeepSeek v3 demonstrates superior performance, achieving a Hit@1 of 93.55% on WikiDiverse and 94.10% on RichpediaMEL. Remarkably, the smaller-scale Qwen3-8B exhibits competitive performance, particularly on the RichpediaMEL dataset, where it achieves a Hit@1 of 94.08%.

⊳\triangleright Embedding Visualization. To verify the View-Specific Experts Module, we visualize expert outputs via t-SNE in Figure 7, corroborating our motivations from three perspectives: 1) As shown in Figures 7(a) and 7(b), the fused outputs generated by the Modality and Granularity expert pools form distinct clusters aligned with their respective input categories (Text vs. Image; Coarse vs. Fine). Despite integrating complementary knowledge from peer experts, the aggregated representations preserve the intrinsic discriminability of the heterogeneous signals. 2) Figure 7(c) demonstrates that experts operate with distinct roles. When provided with identical coarse input, the Coarse (Native) and Fine (Peer) Experts still produce separable output clusters. This indicates that each expert has learned to extract unique semantic features tailored to its specific function, rather than simply replicating the input. 3) Figure 7(d) visualizes the outputs from the Modality, Granularity, and Universal experts given identical input. The formation of three non-overlapping clusters confirms that the Universal Expert successfully captures shared semantics, distinct from the view-specific details captured by the other experts. This disentanglement ensures a comprehensive representation that merges a stable common foundation with context-specific nuances.

⊳\triangleright Complexity Analysis. To evaluate the trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency, we compare the model performance (H@1) against the computational cost (GFLOPs) and model size (parameters) under the WikiDiverse dataset. As illustrated in Figure 8, the proposed method is located in the top-left region, which represents the better balance of high accuracy and low complexity. Existing LLM-based fine-tuning methods, such as IIER, suffer from excessive parameter counts and prohibitive computational overhead. Notably, by incorporating a training-free LLM reranking mechanism, our approach significantly outperforms the IIER method. Additionally, our model outperforms the competitive MMOE and M3EL methods in H@1 while maintaining a comparable or lower computational overhead. Furthermore, the moderate parameter size (indicated by the bubble radius) demonstrates that our approach does not rely on simply scaling up parameters to improve results. Overall, our method achieves a superior trade-off, offering a highly efficient solution for deployment.

5. Conclusion

We proposed the MECI framework to capture multi-level multi-element correspondences for multimodal entity linking. Specifically, to address element dominance in mention-entity correlations, we design a Multi-view Experts Network that employs a “divide-and-conquer” strategy and KL-Guided Routing to decouple feature processing. Meanwhile, to mitigate granularity-level element dominance in cross-modal correlations, we introduce a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module, utilizing dynamic weighting and gating mechanisms to refine interactions. Furthermore, a generative refinement stage leverages LLMs for precise re-ranking. Experiments on WikiMEL, RichpediaMEL, and WikiDiverse confirm MECI’s superiority over state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, the visual information in these datasets is sparse; thus, exploring mechanisms for missing or noisy modalities is an interesting research direction in the future.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
